analytic.title: An edge computing-based monitoring framework for situation-aware embedded real-time systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: An embedded real-time system (ERTS) needs to provide continuous service in various dynamic situations. Such service requirements in different situations create the need for the ERTS to monitor its environment at run time, gather knowledge of its situations, and guarantee its timing and operational behavior through self-adaptation. Recent advances in sensor technologies have introduced cameras, lidar, and radar as powerful monitoring tools. However, processing and storing raw sensor streams require significant storage and computational ability. An ERTS is embedded in nature, and therefore, it has limited storage and processing capacity.

This paper considers that the ERTS contains an analytics endpoint (edge node). We present an edge computing-based monitoring framework that characterizes environmental situations at run time by identifying events and their properties. We enable the framework to store and process from a significantly reduced dataset by creating a knowledge base. The framework also allows the ERTS to identify resource, performance, and safety constraints in the edge node for each situation. The framework assists the ERTS in adapting to the situations (if the constraints are satisfied) by determining adaptive tasks that need to be triggered with respect to the environmental events. The experimental analysis shows that the framework present in the edge node assists in situation characterization in terms of the identified events and admission of adaptive tasks. The monitoring framework also allows improvement regarding the probability of failure and average response time. We use the earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling algorithm with and without considering the edge node and perform a comparative schedulability analysis. We demonstrate that overall demand due to the admission of adaptive tasks and situation-driven analytics exceeds available supply, which can be addressed using the proposed edge computing-based framework.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: An ERTS requires increasing performance and flexibility to support varying requirements obtained from the environment. Such requirements create the necessity to monitor the ERTS environment and apply appropriate adaptations in adverse situations. An ERTS needs to identify different environmental occurrences as events and determine the timing and spatial properties of the events. Data logging can store events in text format. However, sensor data logging is more valuable because it can capture real-world situations at run time with more precision and accuracy [1], but it is associated with additional requirements for processing and storing them. Cloud computing [2] offers to store and process larger files. However, our ability to act on the data might be gone by the time it gets to the cloud for analysis.

With the rise of consumer demands and extensive integration of different IoT and cyber-physical systems in ERTS, the system needs a processing infrastructure that allows deterministic transmission time to ERTS through low-latency network connections. Edge computing recently gained much popularity since the analytics can be performed at end devices [3], which we consider edge nodes. An ERTS with an edge node can allow computations close to the system. If an edge node (having analytics endpoints) is connected to the ERTS, it can provide significantly reduced processing time and network overhead compared to cloud computing.

The ERTS executes a set of system tasks (defined during its design) which we consider high criticality. Such systems must detect different events that can impose safety violations. To handle different situations, the system must be able to execute adaptive tasks (low criticality) in response to environmental events. The system should perform safety, performance, and resource analyses to modify the run time behavior based on those analyses. Therefore, we present an edge computingbased monitoring framework that uses the knowledge base to perform real-time safety, performance, and resource analysis.

The novelty in this research lies in extracting occurrences (real-time) as events through monitoring the sensor input streams of the ERTS. Additionally, we characterize environmental situations from the monitored input streams and create a knowledge base in the edge node. We determine adaptive tasks (in addition to system tasks) which can be activated based on identified environmental events in the current situation. The monitoring framework in the edge node performs a deductive safety analysis that identifies the probability of failure based on the events and components present in the environment at the current situation. The framework determines the performance (response time) in each environmental situation as well as the available resources. The framework evaluates the constraints in each situation. The low criticality identified adaptive tasks are activated and scheduled if the constraints are satisfied.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related existing works along with paper's research objectives. Section 3 describes the system model and assumptions. Section 4 describes the edge computing-based moni-toring framework, which involves characterizing a situation in terms of events, formation of knowledge base, and safety, performance, and resource analysis of the system in the edge node. The experimental analysis of this work is presented in Section 5 and we conclude the paper in Section 6.

div.head: RELATED WORK AND RESEARCH OBJECTIVES
div.p: To the best of our knowledge, a comparable monitoring or verification framework for situation-aware ERTS is absent. However, a number of approaches exist for performing verification/validation of the system at runtime. For assuring the runtime behavior of the system, frameworks like Uppaal [4] validate if the system meets certain timing requirements. Model-checking has been extensively used to validate various hardware and software to ensure expected properties at runtime. A survey on model checking performed in [5] presents that no proper framework exists for modeling (formal) and validation of self-adaptive ERTS. However, we have separate tools for verification and formal modeling.

Much existing work exists for real-time safety analysis, which performs risk assessment based on sensor data [6]. For runtime verification and validation, a number of selfadaptive approaches have been proposed, which are graph transformation-based self-adaptive software systems [7] and the completeness as well as the verification of correctness of self-repairing systems [8]. In goal-oriented approach [9], runtime assurance criteria are defined using goal during system design. Runtime functional behavior in dynamic situations are defined using sub-goals and a decomposition path is identified to meet the expected runtime behavior.

Among existing works, modeling environmental uncertainties into situations are missing. Moreover, identifying events from situations and translating them to adaptive tasks in the edge node based on the identified constraints is also absent. The research objectives of this paper are:
• Identify and track multi-objects from pre-defined environmental region-of interest using Deep SORT and characterize each environmental situation.
• Find adaptive tasks with regard to identified events and identify resource (task demand), performance (response time), and safety (probability of failure) constraints in the edge node.
• If the constraints are satisfied, recommend the ERTS to execute feasible (determined) adaptive tasks.

div.head: SYSTEM MODEL AND ASSUMPTIONS
div.p: The ERTS contains q active real-time system tasks τ sys = {τ sys1 , τ sys2 , . . . , τ sysq } with q ∈ N + . Each system task τ sysi ∈ τ sys is periodic with a period p i > 0. Each system task has criticality C in . The system is connected to the edge node by an Ethernet cable with deterministic worst-case latency L.

Consider that, in the edge node, we receive sensor input I = {I 1 , I 2 , . . . , I n } from the ERTS environment at timestamps T = {T 1 , T 2 , . . . , T n }. An object in this work is defined as an environmental element capable of experiencing any change. The ERTS uses YOLO-LITE [10] to identify objects from Camera and sensor fusion to combine the objects detected from Lidar and Radar. The ERTS also continuously keeps track of the objects using Deep SORT.

An event E i , is defined as an occurrence associated with an object. For example, traffic signals and vehicles in the environment are objects and the changes of locations of vehicles and changes of traffic signals are events. We present an edge computing-based monitoring framework and create a knowledge base called KB. To create KB, we extract different properties of the events identified in the current input stream by using a temporal dataset called EventTempInfo. A situation S i , contains the sequence of identified events along with their properties detected at T i ∈ T.

The ERTS also consists of r active adaptive aperiodic real-time tasks defined as τ out = {τ out1 , τ out2 , . . . , τ outr }. An adaptive real-time task τ outi ∈ τ out , in our system has criticality C out where C in > C out . The proposed monitoring framework in the edge node determines the safety aspects associated with both components and events present in the environment of the ERTS using fault tree analysis. The framework also performs an analysis of the system resource and performance for each situation. The framework evaluates safety, performance, and resource constraints for each situation. If the constraints are satisfied, the framework recommends the ERTS to execute the determined adaptive tasks in addition to the system tasks.

div.head: EDGE COMPUTING-BASED MONITORING FRAMEWORK
div.p: The monitoring framework characterizes environmental situations by defining a region of interest in the environment of the ERTS. In the region of interest, the framework performs identification of objects, tracking the objects using Deep SORT in the subsequent situations, detection as well as extraction of properties of events from the detected events.

div.head: Object identification and tracking using Deep SORT
div.p: In the edge node, the framework identifies the object's location along with its distance from the ERTS using Lidar and RADAR. It uses a camera sensor and captures video streams of the ERTS environment. Sensor fusion is used for combining identified objects from Lidar, Radar, and Camera.

For identifying an object from the video in the current input frame, the framework uses YOLO-LITE [10], which detects class probabilities and bounding box coordinates in each video frame. For tracking an object in different situations, the framework uses Deep SORT [11] algorithm, which uses the Kalman filter to estimate existing tracks using constant velocity and linear observation in the current frame. Object tracking using Deep SORT allows the framework to track and determine changes in the object in subsequent input frames. For each object, it identifies and tracks id, location, state, and speed in the different timestamps.

div.head: Detection of events
div.p: One of the essential tasks in situation characterization is event detection, which involves identifying changes in the tracked object's behavior pattern. For ERTS, delayed computation of the result in many cases, although accurate, have less or no value to the system. To ensure timing guarantees in different situations, the framework determines timing properties associated with each event. To perform efficient extraction of real-time properties, it defines a temporal dataset called EventTempInfo = (timestamp, state, location, id, speed).
At different timestamps of the input frame arrival, the framework stores the state, location, id, and speed of each object.

For each E i , the duration is calculated using EventTempInfo. The framework also uses EventTempInfo to track the event's appearance pattern and determine the event's periodicity (if the event is periodic).

div.head: Discovery of events relationships
div.p: An identified event from a detected object is called a fundamental event E fn . The framework also determines events that occur due to multiple fundamental events. These events are called external events E ex . The framework performs association rule learning to identify external events by defining an association rule set called ExternalRule. Each rule in ExternalRule defines events that have an association among themselves. For identifying external events, the framework determines and selects valid rules out of all rules in ExternalRule. For each fundamental event E fn , the framework, determines its frequency fr(E fn ) in ExternalRule and find all associated external events.

For each associated external event E i ∈ E ex , the framework goes through each occurrence of E fn found in ExternalRule and determines the occurrences where considered external and fundamental value has a true association relationship. It also determines the ratio of true associations with all the associations and determines true relationships fr(E fn ∪ E ex )/fr(E fn ). The framework identifies false relationships, which is a ratio of occurrences where the external events take place without the fundamental events using 1fr(E ex )/1 -trueAssiociation(E fn ). In this work, the framework considers external events which meets a predefined minimum true relationship and maximum false relationships from all possible rules.

div.head: Characterization of environmental situations
div.p: We present KB, which is a knowledge base formed by extracting both timing and spatial properties of the events. For an ERTS, it is essential to generate a dataset that allows the ERTS to understand various patterns and associations among different events. In each arriving frame, the framework identifies different events using temporal data EventTempInfo. For each event, the framework determines whether it was identified in the previous frames using its id from EventTempInfo and distinguishes between new and existing events. For existing events, it also uses EventTempInfo to classify the events.

The framework uses KB to extract the starting time of each current event. In the current input frame, the framework also identifies the event's current location and speed. The framework uses EventTempInfo and ExternalRule to find out information regarding external events using true and false association values.

A situation S i at time T i , in this paper, is events S i = {E 1 , . . . , E m-1 } found from the environment of the ERTS. At time T i , the monitoring framework puts S i , to knowledge base KB i . For i th input frame arrival KB i ∈ KB, can be given as KB i = [T i , S i ]. We store limited situations in KB due to the embedded nature of the edge node. In our work, KB contains 30,000 most recent situations using the First-In-First-Out replacement policy.

div.head: Safety analysis
div.p: For each situation S i , the framework uses a fault tree to identify the probability of failure. Failure, in this case, is defined by the likelihood of an accident taking place in S i . In S i , failure can come through either from events or components. The Bayesian rule is used for identifying failure probability coming from events. This work considers that failure can only come through moving events. Consider that, P(E fn ) is the probability of known motion event E fn and P(E ex ) is the probability of the external event E ex . Also consider that, E ex is derived from E fn . The likelihood of an external event taking place P(E ex ), where E fn has occurred using the Bayesian formula:
div.formula: P(E ex | E fn ) = P(E fn | E ex ) P(E ex ) P(E fn )(1)
div.p: The probability of moving events P(E fn ), is given as:
div.formula: P(E fn ) = Moving events All events(2)
div.p: Calculation of P(E ex ), involves determining motion events in different situations. For situations, S 1 , S 2 , . . . , S i , the framework identifies maximum number of motion events and determines P(E ex ) as a ratio of motion events in the current situation with respect to the maximum number of motion events from previous situations.

The framework also considers the probability of failure coming from components present in the current situation. For each situation, the framework determines the number of components in the environment. Safety integrity level values are used for these calculations. We consider that components present in the environment are SIL 4, of which the worst-case probability of failure value (0.001) is used to determine failure probability. Two or more basic events can lead to different outcomes based on system characteristics. The outcomes can take place if any event occurs or may require every event to occur for the output. The framework multiplies failure probability from events with the failure probability of components to determine the likelihood of failure in the current situation and determine safety constraints.

div.head: Performance and Resource analysis
div.p: For each situation S i , the framework calculates response time with respect to the identification of objects, object tracking, event identification, relationship discovery, identification of adaptive tasks, and communication latency from the edge node to ERTS. The performance constraint for each situation is calculated as the sum of all the response times.

For each situation S i , the framework calculates the worstcase execution time demand for system task τ sys as well as the adaptive tasks τ out . The framework also calculates the accumulated resource demand for both adaptive and system tasks and defines it as a resource constraint. The ERTS allows admission of adaptive tasks if the safety constraints (probability of failure) exceed a pre-defined threshold, the performance constraint (response time) is also below an acceptable threshold and the resource constraint (total time demand for system and adaptive task) is less than the available supply.

div.head: Identification of adaptive tasks
div.p: A task in our work is an execution unit defined as τ i = (α i , c i , d i ) [12] where α i is the arrival time, c i is the execution time, and d i is the task deadline. A real-time adaptive task τ outi ∈ τ out , in ERTS is aperiodic. For situation S i , the framework identifies τ Si out associated with E i using the situation-aware adaptive task model [13]. For characterizing precedence relationships among the adaptive tasks, the framework uses a relationship set PR. Identification of the adaptive tasks is performed through identifying γ = {γ 1 , γ 2 , . . . , γ g }, which are different categories of events detected in S i . We determine adaptive tasks τ Ci out associated with each category C i ∈ C Si which are all possible tasks which can be executed. We also identify the tasks on which τ Ci out is dependant with.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS
div.p: For the experimental analysis, we use A driver assistance ERTS which is a multiprocessor system containing 16 GB RAM, four x64 processors, and 64-bit Ubuntu 16.04 operating system. The considered edge node contains 4GB of RAM and four x64 processors and is connected to the ERTS using a Gigabit Ethernet cable. The edge node contains LIDAR, RADAR, and a Camera sensor, which monitors its runtime environment [13]. For the driver assistance ERTS, the experiment run contains 30,000 situations.

div.head: Formation of Knowledge Base
div.p: The framework detects events by tracking and matching objects from the input streaming data and identifying timing properties (periodicity, duration) and general properties (speed, location, etc.). For each situation, the framework identifies different events detected at that time interval. In this work, the framework detects a total of 1307838 events, out of which 1037154 events are fundamental, and 270684 events are external, while 980382 events are in motion and 327456 are static events.

For each situation, the identified fundamental events, as well as external events along with their properties, are stored in KB. It consumes very less memory in comparison to actual input stream data. For our KB generation experiment, the initial size of the input streams received is 11917513 kilobytes, and KB takes 2578 kilobytes of memory which is significantly less, making it suitable for embedded systems.

div.head: Identification of Safety constraint
div.p: For each situation, the monitoring framework considers the probability of failure as the safety constraint of the ERTS. To identify the safety constraint, the framework performs fault tree analysis. In the fault tree, the framework uses both events identified in the situation as well as elements of the system. For the element-based probability of failure, SIL is used. For event-based failure analysis, the framework identifies the likelihood of a collision based on the events present in the situation (considering only the events which are in motion).

Apart from the identification of the likelihood of failure from fundamental events, the framework uses Equation 2 to identify the failure probability of external events. For each situation, the safety constraint is determined by combining element-based failure as well as the probability of failure coming from both fundamental and external events. Out of 30000 situations, we identify 13112 situations in which the safety constraint is above than the defined safety threshold.

div.head: Identification of Performance and Resource constraint
div.p: The framework considers the response time as the performance constraint. The average analytics overload are 2208, 1795.8, and 1997.3 microseconds for safety, performance, and resource respectively. In 19012 (out of 30000) situations, the performance constraint is below acceptable threshold. Without the edge computing-based monitoring framework, the analysis is performed in the cloud. Sending 30000 raw situational input streams to the cloud generates a very high network overhead. The performance constraint in the edge node is 19881.1 microseconds and 35607.63 microseconds in the cloud.

Resource constraint in this work is the accumulated resource demands of both system and adaptive tasks in a given situation. For each situation, we calculate the maximum supply available after situation characterization and scheduling system tasks. The average available maximum supply in this work is 10118.9 microseconds. In 788 (out of 30000) situations, the resource constraint is below available supply.

div.head: Determining Adaptive tasks
div.p: The framework determines the adaptive tasks with respect to the events in each situation. The adaptive tasks considered this work are: Turn right -90, 60 and 30 degrees, Turn left -90, 60, and 30 degrees, Speed up, Speed down, and brake. For each situation, the framework identifies the adaptive tasks and determines feasibility. Figure 1 shows the resource demands (in nanoseconds) for different situations (sampled with an interval of 200 situations) for the adaptive tasks. In 332 situations (out of 30000), the safety, performance and resource constraints are satisfied altogether. In Figure 1 situations with positive resource demand indicates the constraints were satisfied and those adaptive task were executed where as negative resource demand indicates the situations in which execution of identified adaptive tasks were ignored.

div.head: Scheduling adaptive tasks using EDF
div.p: For the scheduling experiment, each situation is captured every 10000 nanoseconds, which we define as maximum supply. The ERTS itself has a set of pre-defined tasks which it must execute, and the deadline of those tasks cannot be missed. For a particular situation, it is challenging to guarantee that the identification and the analytics overhead will not exceed the supply. Therefore, in parallel, we identify safety, resource, and performance constraints in the edge node. For each situation, if the constraints are satisfied, we use EDF to schedule the system tasks at first, followed by the identified adaptive tasks. For the first 6000 situations, Figure 2 demonstrates the scheduling and analytics overload if the analytics were performed in the ERTS itself rather than the edge node. Figure 2 shows that the addition of these analytics and admission of adaptive tasks sometimes puts the overall overload (scheduling and analytics) to exceed more than the maximum supply and thus makes the ERTS unfeasible. The unfeasibility can be addressed using the edge-driven monitoring framework since the situation characterization, and constraint identification is performed in the edge node. This does not overload the ERTS and allows ERTS admission of adaptive tasks if, for the current situation, the constraints are satisfied.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: We present an edge computing-based monitoring framework by creating KB. The presented framework extracts different patterns involved in the event information from the input. We also obtain real-time properties from the events. KB allows quick information retrieval in shortened memory in the edge node. The framework uses KB to identify performance, safety, and resource constraint for each situation in the edge node.

The framework identifies the adaptive tasks and allows the ERTS to execute them if the safety, performance, and resource constraints are satisfied. The future work of our paper aims to use these analyses in the edge node to find the expected mode, determine system tasks for the expected mode, and adjust the properties of the adaptive tasks to be executed for a given situation based on the expected mode.
